hints: Start by thinking about the bacteria before the antibiotic is added - are they all genetically identical, and if not, where does that original variation come from?
Now think about what the antibiotic does in the environment - does it create the variation, or does it act on variation that is already there?
Compare the fate of two bacteria side by side - one with a variation that helps against the antibiotic and one without - who survives and who reproduces?
Remember this is named as a type of natural selection - which direction is the whole population shifting toward over generations?
Think about how bacteria reproduce so quickly - how is the helpful DNA copy passed to offspring in one cell dividing into two?
Bacteria can also share genes without dividing - recall the three ways DNA can move directly between bacterial cells.
Finish the story at population level - what happens to the frequency of the helpful allele over time, and why does this happen so fast in bacteria plus how does misuse of antibiotics make it worse?
walkthrough:
Variation Comes First By Random Mutation**
Bacteria do not become resistant because they need to. Random mutation in DNA happens spontaneously during replication and creates new alleles. In a large population, a few cells by chance already carry an allele coding for resistance, for example an enzyme that breaks down the antibiotic or a changed target protein.

Antibiotic Is The Selection Pressure**
When antibiotic is used, it creates a new environment. This is directional selection. It does not cause the mutation, it selects between variants already present. Non-resistant bacteria are killed or prevented from growing, while resistant bacteria have a selective advantage in this environment.

Survival, Reproduction And Change In Allele Frequency**
Only resistant bacteria survive to reproduce and pass on the resistance allele to offspring. Susceptible alleles are removed. Over generations the frequency of the resistance allele increases until the population is mainly resistant. That is evolution by natural selection.

Why Resistance Spreads So Fast In Bacteria**
Vertical transmission is very fast because bacteria reproduce asexually by binary fission with a short generation time, so one resistant cell quickly forms a large clone. Horizontal transmission speeds it up even more - resistance genes on plasmids can pass between living bacteria by conjugation, or by transformation from dead cells, or by transduction by viruses. Overuse of antibiotics or stopping a course early leaves some bacteria alive and increases the chance that resistant survivors multiply.

Final answer: Random mutation produces variation including an allele for antibiotic resistance. Antibiotic acts as selection pressure for directional selection. Bacteria with resistance allele have selective advantage, so survive and reproduce while non-resistant die. Resistance passed on by vertical transmission in binary fission and by horizontal transmission in conjugation / transformation / transduction. Frequency of resistance allele increases to give resistant population. Short generation time gives rapid evolution, worsened by overuse or not completing antibiotic course.
